analysis.one_liner: Strengthens black lung benefits for coal miners: faster claims, paid attorney fees, free medical exams, and stricter evidence rules for operators.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, markup, or vote — it sat in two House committees from April 2017 until the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Black Lung Benefits Act to make it easier for coal miners disabled by black lung disease — and their surviving spouses — to win benefits. It requires coal companies to hand over all medical evidence in a claim, pays miners' attorney fees from the disability trust fund, gives miners free lung evaluations and CT scans, toughens the presumptions that establish disability, indexes the benefit to inflation, and lets previously denied claims be reopened. It also directs a study of whether mine dust limits should be tightened further, and creates criminal penalties and disqualification for anyone — including company lawyers and doctors — who falsifies or hides evidence in a claim.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal miners with black lung disease and their surviving spouses and dependents. A miner with complicated pneumoconiosis would be presumed totally disabled without needing to fight through adversarial litigation; a miner with 15 or more years underground would get a rebuttable presumption with less medical proof. Claimants whose cases drag past a year would have attorney fees and case-building medical expenses paid from the trust fund rather than out of pocket — the bill's own findings note only 33% of claimants have a lawyer at the initial stage. Miners whose claims were denied on x-ray readings by a physician the Labor Department later deemed not credible could refile within a year, with benefits backdated. Miners would also get free complete pulmonary evaluations and CT scans, with physicians who work for coal companies or their law firms screened out for conflicts of interest.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal miners with black lung disease

how_it_helps.text: The Labor Department would pay attorneys' fees (up to $4,500) and unreimbursed medical expenses (up to $3,000) from the trust fund for contested claims that have not reached a final decision within a year, and the liable coal operator must reimburse the fund if the claimant wins.

Operators would have to deliver a copy of any company-ordered medical examination report within 21 days and share all medical information they develop, even evidence they do not plan to use — the bill's findings state some operators' lawyers have withheld evidence that would have substantiated miners' claims.

A miner with progressive massive fibrosis (a large opacity over 1 centimeter) would face an irrebuttable presumption of total disability, and miners with 15+ years in coal mines would get a rebuttable presumption of total disability from the disease.
If the evidence on an issue is evenly balanced, the adjudicator must resolve the doubt in the claimant's favor.

Claimants could request a free complete pulmonary evaluation paid for by the fund, CT scans for suspected complicated disease, and an impartial NIOSH panel to classify chest x-rays when the diagnosis is disputed — with conflict-of-interest screening excluding physicians employed or retained by the opposing party or its lawyers in the prior 24 months.
The annual benefit would be raised to $7,980 beginning 2015 and indexed to inflation, replacing a formula tied to federal pay rates that had frozen miners' cost-of-living increases.

Knowingly false statements or misrepresentation in a black lung case would carry up to 5 years' imprisonment, and attorneys or expert witnesses who commit such conduct would be permanently disqualified from black lung cases; judges could sanction parties who refuse to produce evidence.

Claimants or survivors denied benefits on readings by a physician whose negative x-ray interpretations the Labor Department directed 'not be credited' could refile within one year, and awards would be backdated to the original denial or the miner's death.

The Labor Department would have to use continuous personal dust monitor data in a retrospective study of whether to lower the respirable coal dust and silica limits, and revise the standards if the study says the disease rate has not fallen.
Black lung clinics could use federal funds to help miners and their families file claims, and Department of Labor adjudicators would receive annual training on the medical evidence.

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators. Benefit payments and the new fee-and-expense program come from the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, and operators found liable must reimburse the fund for the fees, medical expenses, and evaluation costs when a claimant wins — plus the underlying benefits. Operators also bear the cost of mandatory disclosure of their medical evidence, potential attorney disqualification and sanctions for withholding it, and, if the study recommends it, tighter dust limits and more frequent sampling.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal mine operators, via the trust fund

drawbacks.text: The benefit increase, easier presumptions, and reopened claims would raise program costs substantially. The trust fund is financed by an excise tax on coal, so the added liability falls on coal operators and, to the extent they pass it through, on coal prices — in coal-dependent regions this is a real economic cost.

Reopening previously denied claims — including surviving family members' claims — with backdated payments extends operators' liability years into the past, which industry would argue punishes companies for diagnoses that were legitimately contested at the time.

The bill raises the stakes of every claim on both sides: permanent disqualification from black lung practice for a single knowing false statement, and default decisions against a party that fails to produce evidence. Supporters would counter that these mirror the asymmetry the bill's findings describe, where only 33% of claimants have an attorney at the initial stage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are real but bounded: fee payments are capped at $4,500 per claim and the operator reimburses the fund whenever a claim succeeds, so the fund is not the long-run loser. The larger costs to operators — more successful claims, backdated awards, tighter possible dust limits — are precisely the point of the bill: a program meant to pay disabled miners was, in the sponsors' findings, letting companies win through resource disparities, withheld evidence, and questionable x-ray readings. For a disease that has killed more than 76,000 miners since 1968 and is now striking younger miners in advanced form, the bill's costs track the harm the program was created to cover. The main honest caveat is the cost imposed on coal-dependent regional economies, which the bill does not offset.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce and Ways and Means committees on the day it was introduced, and neither committee ever took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Cartwright introduced the bill on April 5, 2017, joined by Reps. Bobby Scott of Virginia and Frederica Wilson of Florida as original sponsors.
It was referred that day to two committees, Education and the Workforce and Ways and Means, for consideration of the provisions under each committee's jurisdiction.
The complete action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — for the remainder of the Congress.
Five additional Democratic representatives cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal mine operators are better off because the bill died: they avoided the expanded benefit liabilities, mandatory disclosure of their medical evidence, potential dust-limit tightening, and the risk that claims denied on discredited x-ray readings would be reopened with backdated awards. Disabled miners and their survivors gained nothing from the Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal mine operators and their lawyers

against.name: Coal mine operators
against.role: Liable payers under the Black Lung Benefits Act
against.what_they_did: Coal companies had a documented record of contesting black lung claims and, per the bill's own findings, having lawyers and company-retained doctors withhold or skew medical evidence; the bill would have imposed new disclosure, fee, and reimbursement obligations on them. No operator publicly championed the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so there is no roll-call record, but all six original sponsors were Democrats and none of the bill's five cosponsors was a Republican; the Republican chairs of both receiving committees took no action on it.

industries.note: Operators would owe benefits in more cases, reimburse the trust fund for claimants' fees and medical costs, disclose all their medical evidence, face attorney-disqualification and sanction rules, and potentially operate under lower dust and silica limits. The bill's findings describe operators' representatives withholding evidence and company-retained doctors systematically misclassifying x-rays to defeat claims.

industries.industry: Physicians and B readers retained by coal operators
industries.note: The bill would bar physicians employed or retained by the opposing party or its law firms (within 24 months) from doing claimant evaluations, and replace partisan x-ray readings with an impartial NIOSH panel for disputed diagnoses — eliminating a paid role in opposing claims. The bill's findings state the Labor Department had already stopped crediting negative readings by one widely used physician.
Clinics could use federal funds to help miners, spouses, and dependents file claims, in addition to providing respiratory care.

A new payment program would pay capped attorney fees for contested claims unresolved within a year, with the operator reimbursing the fund on a win — addressing the finding that only 33% of claimants have counsel at the initial stage.
